You raise a fair question. If I may explain:

Monopolies / oligopolies don't naturally exist in the long term without government interference.

It is possible to have a monopoly in the short term due to a sudden jump in technological capability or a short term willingness to sell your product at a loss. But, over the longer term, competition will come in and sort things out. This is the natural order of free markets.

BUT, once a government protects an industry through regulations, tariffs, barriers to entry, right of way access rules, special tax rules, so called 'universal access' rules, etc. Then things become unbalanced. We've seen this in banking, telecom, etc. We see this in the media industry through broadcast licenses, preferential access for reporters, direct payments (it's ridiculous - our government spends major $$ on advertising), etc.

So, when a government comes in and breaks up an monopoly / oligopoly they are just undoing past mistakes. Do two wrongs make a right? Maybe, but it's difficult to say.

In my opinion, on this specific issue: I don't think we need to see break-up of the media - thanks to the internet we have free and open alternatives to the controlled corporate media. The corporate media is dying ... let it die.

Also: one other point: There are 2 types of deregulation. Real deregulation intended to open up markets and make things more free. And fake deregulation which is just crony capitalism. Fake deregulation involves giving existing powerful players more freedom but still keeping the barriers to entry to protect these same players. What comes from Washington (in the last ~40 years) is always 'fake deregulation'. (We have seen some nice 'real' deregulation at the state level. That's where most of the freedom gains have been made...)
